r: SED 1009 pairs trained academic coaches with students to build executive-functioning skills: goal-setting, time management, task initiation, and study-strategy selection, delivered through an ongoing individualized coaching relationship. AI study-planning tools already draft schedules, flashcards, and study guides competently, and task-exposure research finds writing and structured-advice generation positively associated with AI exposure. But the applied work here is not producing a study plan; it is a sustained coaching relationship that reads a specific student's motivation, executive-function profile, and setbacks in real time and adjusts support session to session. Observed-usage data shows coaching and mentoring interactions remain a smaller share of automated usage than drafting and analysis tasks. With no licensure gate and no general-studies designation protecting it, this course's instrumental case rests on that relational, adaptive coaching core, which near-term AI assistants can supplement but do not yet replace.

By 2031, AI coaching companions will plausibly handle more of the routine scaffolding this course teaches, generating personalized study schedules, tracking assignment deadlines, and prompting reflection questions, extending the productivity gains observed in professional-writing research toward student-facing coaching tools. Diffusion data suggests such tools will be common but not universal across campuses. The course's protective core weakens: much of what an academic coach explains can be delivered adequately by an AI tutor for many students, particularly those with milder executive-functioning needs. Yet students who most need this course, those struggling with motivation, self-regulation, or crisis derailment, still benefit from a human who notices patterns an automated check-in misses and who can escalate concerns. The rating rises to Medium, reflecting genuine but partial erosion: coaching content becomes more AI-deliverable while the human relationship retains real, if narrowing, value for the hardest cases.

A decade out, under a central-case capability trajectory where task-time horizons continue doubling every few months, AI coaching systems could plausibly conduct most routine executive-functioning coaching competently, including personalized check-ins and adaptive strategy recommendations, given how strongly writing and advice-generation tasks track with AI exposure. Diffusion into student-support infrastructure is far less certain than the underlying capability, and colleges have historically been slow adopters of automated advising relative to industry. No licensure or foundational constraint holds this course in place, so if the capability materializes and campuses deploy it broadly, the instrumental case for a dedicated coaching course erodes substantially. The rating moves to High, but with real uncertainty: an entirely automated version of this individualized, trust-dependent relationship for at-risk students has not been demonstrated, and the projection should be read as directional rather than firm.
SED 1009.d: This course couples learning strategies with executive functioning coaching to develop the study and executive functioning skills needed for academic and workplace success. Students and academic coaches will work together to discover and practice tools and strategies to reach each student's academic potential with individualized support.

r: SED 2200 asks pre-service teachers to analyze how institutional oppression, privilege, and whiteness shape outcomes for culturally and linguistically diverse students with disabilities, using readings, case studies, and reflective writing to build advocacy skills. Task-exposure research finds writing tasks strongly positively associated with AI exposure, and a general-purpose model can already draft competent policy critiques or reflection essays on these themes. That pushes exposure upward. But the course's substantive work is positionality-aware critical analysis and classroom advocacy planning grounded in a candidate's own social location, output an AI cannot supply on the student's behalf without misrepresenting lived experience, and instructors specifically assess authentic reflection rather than polished prose. As a program-required course contributing to the special-education endorsement sequence without a hard course-specific licensure mandate, near-term diffusion into teacher-prep curricula remains limited. The rating holds Low at 24 months, protected mainly by adoption lag and the reflective, identity-grounded nature of the work.

By 2031, AI drafting assistance for policy analysis, case-study response papers, and advocacy plans will be widespread and competent, consistent with the trajectory professional-writing productivity research already shows for time savings and quality gains. The instrumental case for the informational content of this course weakens: a student could plausibly have AI generate defensible analyses of deficit narratives or inequitable policy structures. What is harder to automate is the critical self-examination the course requires, interrogating one's own privilege and practice, which functions as an assessed, personal deliverable rather than a generic essay. As a program-mandated but not board-named course, its curricular position could shift somewhat within five years if faculty lean more heavily on AI-assisted analysis exercises. The rating rises to Medium, reflecting real erosion in the informational and writing component balanced against the persistently human, reflective core the course is designed to cultivate.

Over a decade, capability growth of the kind projected by task-time-horizon research makes it plausible that AI can produce sophisticated, well-sourced critical analyses of educational equity, disability policy, and systemic oppression on demand, matching or exceeding typical student writing. With no embodiment, no hard licensure mandate, and no foundational role gating later required courses, little in this course's structure resists that trend at the ten-year horizon. The rating moves to High, hedged substantially: ten-year forecasts carry wide uncertainty, program requirements could be redesigned around AI-assisted critical reflection rather than replaced by it, and authentic first-person positionality work may retain assessed value even as AI handles the surrounding research and drafting. This should be read as a directional statement about instrumental exposure of the informational content, not a claim that critical social-justice literacy becomes unnecessary.
SED 2200.d: Students conceptualize social justice concepts related to the impact of institutional oppressions on culturally, racially, and linguistically diverse students with disabilities. Students engage in course activities and discussion on unequal power dynamics, privilege, and the presence of whiteness within educational institutions. Through readings, projects, case studies and discussions, students analyze the historical, legal, and socio-cultural context that perpetuates inequities. Students reflect on their role as changemakers in the context of schools, and critically analyze historic and current policies, laws, and societal deficit narratives related to different marginalized groups. Students prepare to be changemakers by applying social justice concepts of resistance, advocacy, and activism.

r: SED 2700 surveys the historical development and major concepts of special-education services for students with social, emotional, and behavioral difficulties, building candidates' foundational vocabulary for later disability-specific judgment. Much of this content, definitions, historical timelines, disorder categories, is exactly the kind of structured explanatory material task-exposure research associates with high AI exposure, since general conceptual explanation and synthesis is well within current model competence. A capable model can already summarize this material accurately. However, the course exists inside the special-education endorsement's required content sequence rather than being a hard board-named clinical course, and its knowledge underwrites later applied judgment about real students with real legal stakes. At 24 months, limited classroom AI diffusion and the course's program-mandated role keep the rating Low: the conceptual content is exposed, but its instrumental role in the licensure pathway is not yet displaced.

By 2031, AI tutoring and explanatory tools will plausibly deliver this course's core conceptual content, disorder categories, historical context, basic diagnostic concepts, as competently as a textbook or lecture, extending the pattern observed-usage data already shows for education and explanatory tasks. That materially erodes the pure knowledge-transmission rationale for a dedicated course. What is not displaced is the requirement that special-education candidates demonstrate this foundational competence as part of an accredited, program-mandated sequence feeding state licensure, and the application of these concepts to actual children carries real verification stakes that a five-year AI-literacy gap does not resolve. The rating rises to Medium: the informational content is increasingly AI-deliverable, while the course's place in the required curriculum and its link to applied disability judgment provide a partial, not complete, brake on erosion.

A decade out, under continued rapid capability growth, AI conceivably delivers this course's conceptual material, and even scaffolds case-based application exercises, at a level indistinguishable from current instruction, consistent with aggressive central-case trajectories for task automation. Because this is a program-contributory content course rather than a hard-licensed clinical requirement, and it does not itself gate other required courses in this sequence, the institutional brake here is comparatively soft. The rating moves to High, but the projection should be treated cautiously: state approval processes for special-education endorsement curricula move slowly, disability-specific concept application still requires human judgment when real students are involved, and a ten-year capability forecast for a nuanced, ethically-weighted topic like disability categorization carries substantial uncertainty in both directions.
SED 2700.d: This course provides an overview of the major concepts and historical antecedents of special education services for children and youth with social, emotional, and behavioral difficulties. Teacher candidates will develop an understanding of basic concepts related to the social, emotional, and behavioral development of children and youth, and the concepts related to disordered behavior.

r: SED 3050 trains candidates to select, administer, interpret, and report formal and informal special-education assessments, culminating in a series of actual assessment reports. This maps to evaluating information against standards and interpreting results for others, work with direct legal consequence, since eligibility, present-levels, and IEP goal-setting under IDEA hinge on defensible, individualized interpretation. AI drafting tools can already generate report templates and summarize scores, giving real but partial exposure. The binding constraint is verification burden: an incorrect eligibility or present-levels determination has high error cost and can trigger due-process disputes, so oversight strictly requires a human holding this specific assessment knowledge, precisely the jagged-frontier condition where ungrounded AI trust produces measurably worse outcomes. Layered onto that is the course's place inside the CDE-approved special-education endorsement curriculum. At 24 months the rating is Low, protected by both verification demands and licensure structure.

By 2031, AI will plausibly draft substantial portions of assessment reports from raw score data and observational notes, and productivity research on professional writing already shows large time savings with quality gains for exactly this kind of structured-document work. That meaningfully automates the mechanical reporting task. It does not automate the judgment of which assessments are valid for a given student, how to interpret discrepant data, or how to write legally defensible present-levels statements, decisions with high stakes and non-obvious failure modes that keep a knowledgeable human in the loop. The accredited endorsement curriculum's assessment-competency requirement does not relax on a five-year clock. The rating remains Low: report drafting increasingly automates, but the interpretive and legally consequential core of the course, protected by both verification burden and licensure structure, keeps the instrumental need for the course largely intact.

Over ten years, AI assessment-support tools could become deeply embedded in special-education practice, handling scoring, drafting, and even flagging inconsistencies with strong reliability, consistent with aggressive capability-growth trajectories. The institutional cap can relax at this horizon: a decade is enough time for licensure bodies to revise how assessment competency is demonstrated, matching the pattern seen in other accredited-curriculum courses where the mandate cap loosens only at the ten-year mark. The rating moves to Medium, the mechanical and much of the interpretive workload becomes highly automatable, while final determinations affecting a child's legal educational rights plausibly still require a credentialed human's sign-off. This is a genuinely uncertain projection: due-process and disability-rights litigation risk could just as easily harden verification requirements as loosen them over a decade.
SED 3050.d: This course focuses on making informed decisions on the selection, use, and interpretation of formal and informal methods for the assessment of students with disabilities. Teacher candidates must complete a series of special education assessments and reports during this course.

r: SED 3100 has candidates build individualized communication plans for students with communication challenges, with particular attention to students with autism and significant support needs whose access to instruction depends on getting augmentative and alternative communication supports right. The applied task, assessing a specific student's communication modality and drafting a collaborative plan, carries real stakes: a poorly matched communication plan can cut a student off from instruction and peers entirely, a high-error-cost, non-obvious failure mode that keeps a knowledgeable human in the loop. AI drafting tools can already suggest generic AAC frameworks, giving partial exposure, but the course explicitly emphasizes cross-team collaboration to fit the plan to the individual child. As a required methods course inside the special-education endorsement sequence, near-term adoption of AI-authored communication plans in practice is minimal. The rating is Low at 24 months, held by verification burden and program requirement together.

By 2031, AI communication-support tools, including AAC recommendation engines and speech-generating device configuration assistants, will likely be more embedded in special-education practice, and observed productivity gains from AI assistance for novices suggest they could meaningfully help less-experienced teachers draft initial communication plans. That is real automation of a first-pass task. The plan still must be validated against a specific child's sensory, motor, and social profile through direct observation and interdisciplinary collaboration, exactly the kind of embodied, real-time judgment that resists full delegation, and a mismatched recommendation carries high cost for a vulnerable learner. The methods-course mandate inside the endorsement sequence does not loosen on a five-year cycle. The rating stays Low: AI increasingly assists drafting, but the verification-heavy, collaborative core of individualized communication planning keeps the course's instrumental role largely intact.

A decade out, more sophisticated multimodal AI could plausibly analyze video or sensor data of a student's communicative attempts and propose increasingly well-calibrated AAC plans, extending current trajectories in assistive-technology capability. Because this is a strong program mandate rather than a hard board-named clinical requirement with fixed clock hours, the institutional cap loosens somewhat by ten years under the deterministic rule. The rating rises to Medium: substantial drafting and pattern-recognition work becomes automatable, while direct observation of a child's real-time communicative behavior and the collaborative judgment to adapt a plan as the child changes remain resistant to full substitution. This carries real uncertainty, both the pace of assistive-technology adoption in under-resourced schools and the willingness of IEP teams to rely on AI-generated recommendations for the most vulnerable students are open questions.
SED 3100.d: Communication is the foundation for all learning. In this course, participants will consider natural and meaningful communicative engagement in inclusive settings and will create communication plans for students with communication challenges. All modes of communication and all language levels will be addressed. There will be a focus on the communication needs of students with autism and significant support needs (SSN) because the communication plan for these students may require the most collaboration for successful inclusion.

r: SED 3250 teaches applied behavior analysis, functional behavior assessment, and behavior intervention planning, and requires a 15-hour field experience applying Universal Design for Learning in real classrooms. The field component is direct, in-person work with actual students exhibiting challenging behavior, observation, data collection, and real-time intervention, squarely in the low-exposure, high-presence task categories task-exposure research identifies. Behavior intervention plans also carry high error cost: a poorly designed plan can escalate a crisis or violate a student's rights, so verification strictly requires a human holding this knowledge. AI can already help draft generic FBA templates, a modest exposure, but cannot conduct the classroom observation or manage the real-time behavioral event the field hours require. At 24 months the rating is Low, protected jointly by the embodied field requirement and the behavior-analysis verification burden.

By 2031, AI behavior-tracking and data-visualization tools will plausibly help teachers log antecedents, behaviors, and consequences more efficiently, and generate draft intervention strategies from behavioral data patterns, a real augmentation of the analytic side of this course. But the field-experience requirement itself, and the embodied skill of observing and responding to a live behavioral event with a specific child, is not something a five-year capability gain touches; that remains presence-dependent, real-time, interpersonal work. The verification burden around behavior plans affecting a child's placement or discipline record stays high. Field-hour requirements inside teacher-preparation programs do not relax on a catalog-revision timescale. The rating remains Low: AI increasingly assists the paperwork and data analysis, while the supervised, in-person behavioral competence at the course's core, and the stakes of getting it wrong, keep the instrumental need for the course intact.

Even under an aggressive ten-year capability trajectory, the requirement that teacher candidates complete supervised, in-person field hours applying behavioral principles with real students is among the more durable constraints in a teacher-preparation catalog, comparable to other field-experience anchors where embodiment and licensure-adjacent program structure jointly hold the rating down. The genuine uncertainty is in how much of the surrounding behavioral-data analysis and intervention drafting becomes AI-assisted, plausibly a great deal, following trends in adjacent analytic tasks. But the field hours and the real-time judgment of a live behavioral crisis with a specific child are not delegable to AI in the central case by 2036. The rating holds Low with reasonably high confidence, anchored by the explicit clock-hour field requirement embedded directly in the course description.
SED 3250.d: Students in this course are introduced to the principles of applied behavior analysis and behavior modification. The use of systematic behavioral assessments, functional behavior assessment plans, behavior intervention plans, and classroom intervention strategies are emphasized. Teacher candidates are prepared to apply Universal Design for Learning (UDL) principles in diverse contexts that include both general and special education classes. This course includes a 15-hour field experience.

r: SED 3300 has pre-service teachers examine collective efficacy and collaboration and practice designing student-centered, trauma-informed, inclusive lessons and learning environments. Lesson and environment design is one of the more AI-exposed teaching tasks: task-exposure research finds writing and structured-content generation strongly positively associated with exposure, and general-purpose models already draft passable trauma-informed lesson outlines. That gives real near-term exposure to the drafting side of the course. The course's substantive work, though, is collaborative practice, building the interpersonal skill of collective efficacy with peers and applying it live in a specific classroom culture, which is not equivalent to producing a lesson document. As a course required in sequence with the program's foundational exceptionality course but without a hard board-named mandate, near-term diffusion into teacher-prep pedagogy courses is still limited. The rating is Low at 24 months, held mainly by adoption lag and the collaborative-practice core.

By 2031, AI lesson-planning and environment-design assistance will likely be commonplace in teacher preparation, consistent with observed productivity gains for professional writing and drafting tasks, meaningfully reducing the time candidates spend generating the artifacts this course teaches them to produce. That substantially automates the drafting component. The course's practiced collaboration, building collective efficacy with colleagues, applying student-centered and trauma-informed judgment in a live classroom with real learners, is a real-time interpersonal skill that AI assistance augments rather than performs. This course sits in the program's required sequence without a hard clinical-hour mandate protecting it, so the cap on its rating loosens once drafting is substantially automated. The rating rises to Medium, reflecting genuine erosion of the content-generation task balanced against the collaborative-practice skill the course still requires candidates to demonstrate.

A decade out, under continued rapid capability growth in language and reasoning tasks, AI could plausibly generate highly individualized, trauma-informed lesson and environment designs on demand, further eroding the informational core of this course, consistent with aggressive central-case trajectories for task-time-horizon growth. The program-mandate cap identified for this course holds the rating at Medium rather than releasing it further, since the course remains a required, if not board-named, component of the special-education endorsement sequence and diffusion of fully autonomous lesson design into licensure-track programs is uneven. The rating holds Medium: the lesson-and-environment-design content becomes highly AI-generatable, but the applied, collaborative classroom practice the course assesses, and its place in a state-approved program sequence, keep it from reaching High. Ten-year forecasts for how teacher-prep programs restructure around AI-assisted lesson design carry real uncertainty in either direction.
SED 3300.d: In this course, pre-service teachers will work collaboratively to meet the diverse needs of all learners. Responsive pedagogy connects the learner and the content in meaningful, respectful and effective ways. Participants will examine the principles of collective efficacy and collaboration and practice using the skills necessary to create lessons and learning environments based on student-centered instruction and inclusive and trauma-informed practices.

r: SED 3550 introduces candidates to collaboratively creating meaningful learning environments and authentic engagement supports, across people and settings, for students with significant and diverse needs. The applied work is coordinative and relational, building cross-setting supports with families, related-service providers, and school teams around a specific student's engagement, which maps to team-coordination and interpersonal-communication activities that task-exposure research places among the less-exposed categories relative to routine writing. AI can already help draft generic support-plan language, a modest exposure, but cannot conduct the collaborative, in-person coordination across settings the course centers. As a program-required course inside the special-education endorsement sequence without a hard clinical clock-hour mandate, near-term classroom AI diffusion is limited. The rating is Low at 24 months, protected by the collaborative, cross-setting coordination work and the course's program-mandated position.

By 2031, AI planning tools will plausibly help draft engagement and support-plan templates more efficiently, extending productivity gains observed in professional documentation tasks to special-education planning paperwork. That automates a meaningful slice of the paperwork side of the course. What resists automation is the coordinative work itself, building authentic, trusting collaboration among family members, related-service providers, and general-education staff around a student with significant needs, and adapting the plan as circumstances change across real settings. That interpersonal coordination carries genuine verification stakes when engagement supports fail a vulnerable student. The program mandate holding this course in the endorsement sequence does not relax within a five-year catalog cycle. The rating remains Low, with the paperwork-drafting task increasingly AI-assisted while the collaborative, cross-setting core of the course keeps its instrumental role largely intact.

Over ten years, broader AI diffusion into case coordination, flagging gaps in service plans, summarizing team input, tracking engagement data across settings, could substantially reduce the administrative burden this course's content addresses, consistent with aggressive central-case capability trajectories. Because the course is a strong program mandate rather than a hard board-named clinical requirement, the institutional cap loosens at the ten-year horizon under the deterministic rule. The rating rises to Medium: much of the coordinative paperwork becomes AI-assisted, while the trust-building, cross-setting collaboration with families and multidisciplinary teams around a student with significant needs remains a real-time interpersonal skill that resists full delegation. This is a genuinely uncertain long-horizon projection, particularly given how unevenly AI tools diffuse into already under-resourced special-education service coordination.
SED 3550.d: This course introduces pre-service teachers to inclusive education for students with significant and diverse needs. The focus is on collaboratively creating meaningful learning environments in schools and communities and providing supports for authentic engagement across people and settings.

r: SED 3600 is the gateway course of the special-education sequence: using a case-study method, candidates learn to make instructional decisions about students across the full range of disability and giftedness categories, calibrated to their licensure level. Six other required courses in the program list this course as prerequisite or corequisite, making it a critical foundational substrate the rest of the sequence depends on. The applied task, reasoning through a case to a defensible instructional decision, carries real stakes, since misapplied disability categorization affects a child's placement and services, keeping verification burden high. AI can already summarize disability categories and even draft plausible case responses, a real exposure to the informational layer, but the course's foundational, program-anchoring role and its link to real decisions about children hold the rating down. The rating is Low at 24 months, doubly protected by foundational lock-in and verification demands.

By 2031, AI case-analysis tools will plausibly generate competent first-pass instructional recommendations from case descriptions, extending the pattern seen in professional-writing productivity research to case-based coursework. That meaningfully automates the informational and analytical layer of the course. What does not change is its structural position: because it gates enrollment in the program's other required special-education courses, any curricular redesign has to happen deliberately and slowly, and the case-based judgment about real children's placement and services still carries a verification burden that makes ungrounded reliance on AI recommendations risky, consistent with jagged-frontier findings on miscalibrated trust outside a model's competence zone. The rating stays Low: case-analysis content becomes more AI-generatable, but the course's foundational role anchoring the rest of the sequence, plus its stakes-laden subject matter, keep the instrumental case largely intact.

A decade out, under continued rapid capability growth, AI could plausibly perform sophisticated case-based reasoning about disability categories and instructional decisions at a level approaching the informational content this course teaches. The foundational-scaffolding cap relaxes only to Medium at this horizon under the deterministic rule, reflecting that a course anchoring six other required courses is unlikely to be eliminated outright even if its content becomes largely AI-deliverable, more likely it is restructured around AI-assisted case work than removed. The rating rises to Medium: the case-study content is highly exposed to capability growth, while the course's structural role as the sequence's foundation and the real stakes of disability-related decisions provide a genuine, if partial, brake. Ten-year program-redesign outcomes are inherently uncertain and could move in either direction.
SED 3600.d: SED 3600 was designed to introduce students to exceptionality in the classroom from an educational decision- making perspective. Information regarding disabilities and giftedness is presented in a manner to familiarize students with the many instructional decisions they must be prepared to make on the basis of the diversity of the classroom population. The case study method is the approach that will be used in this course. Students will be expected to apply course content to solve various problems that are presented within the context of case studies. These case studies will be specific to the student's level of teacher licensure and will provide exposure to relevant issues pertaining to early childhood, elementary, or secondary education.

r: SED 3625 teaches instructional methods and strategies for the academic, behavioral, and social needs of students with disabilities, covering lesson planning, classroom structure, and behavior-management systems. Lesson planning and strategy generation are among the more AI-exposed teaching tasks, and generative tools already draft passable differentiated lesson outlines, giving real near-term exposure. But applying these strategies to a specific student's disability profile, and managing the classroom structure and behavior system in real time with actual children, is embodied, real-time, and carries genuine verification stakes, an ill-fitted behavioral or instructional strategy can worsen outcomes for a vulnerable learner, keeping a knowledgeable human in the loop. As a required methods course inside the CDE-approved special-education endorsement sequence, its curricular position is not something a two-year AI-diffusion window changes. The rating is Low at 24 months, held by both verification burden and licensure structure.

By 2031, AI lesson- and strategy-drafting tools will plausibly generate individualized instructional plans and behavior-management templates efficiently, consistent with productivity research showing large gains for structured drafting tasks. That automates a meaningful share of the planning workload this course teaches. Implementing and adjusting a classroom management and instructional-strategy system in real time with students who have disabilities remains embodied, presence-dependent work that a five-year capability gain does not eliminate, and getting behavioral strategy wrong for a specific student carries real cost. The methods-course mandate inside the accredited endorsement sequence does not loosen on a five-year cycle. The rating stays Low: strategy drafting becomes substantially AI-assisted, while the applied, in-classroom implementation and the licensure-linked verification burden keep the course's instrumental role largely intact through this horizon.

Over ten years, under an aggressive central-case capability trajectory, AI could plausibly generate highly individualized instructional and behavioral strategy plans and even simulate classroom scenarios for practice, but the requirement that CDE-approved special-education endorsement candidates demonstrate this instructional-methods competence is unlikely to be fully retired by 2036, even as licensure bodies could revise how competency is demonstrated at this long horizon under sustained capability growth. The rating rises to Medium, reflecting that strategy generation becomes highly automatable while the real-time classroom implementation and its accreditation-linked verification requirement provide a partial, lower-bound brake consistent with how the deterministic rule treats a hard course-specific mandate at the ten-year mark. This projection should be read with real uncertainty about how licensure requirements and classroom-management practice actually evolve over a decade.
SED 3625.d: This course will introduce the pre-service teacher to components of effective instructional methods and strategies related to supporting the academic, behavioral, and social needs of students with disabilities. Topics explored during the class will focus on the history of special education in schools and learning theories related to becoming a teacher, supporting the behavioral needs of students through setting up your classroom structure and management system, lesson planning, and creating inclusive environments within schools.

r: This course teaches special education law history, the referral-to-IEP pipeline, procedural safeguards, and case-study IEP drafting -- tasks mapping to interpreting information for others and documenting/recording information rather than physical execution. Generative tools already draft boilerplate IEP goals and summarize statutes, so some drafting mechanics are within reach, yet task-exposure research notes that science and critical-thinking skills are negatively associated with exposure, and applying procedural safeguards to an individual student's due-process rights is exactly that kind of judgment. Verification burden is severe: an incorrect IEP or safeguards violation invites due-process litigation, so oversight requires a human who actually understands the law. The binding constraint is Colorado's board-approved special education endorsement curriculum, which specifies this content as required coursework. At 24 months the instrumental need to master this material personally is essentially untouched; AI assists drafting but does not certify legal competence.

By 2031, AI drafting assistants embedded in IEP-management platforms will likely handle more of the mechanical documentation -- populating present-levels statements, generating goal banks, flagging missing procedural elements. Observed-usage data already shows writing and office-document tasks as a leading application category, consistent with that trajectory. But the course's core competency is judging whether a proposed IEP is legally defensible and individually appropriate for a specific child, a high-stakes, adversarial-review context where the jagged-frontier finding on miscalibrated trust outside a system's competence zone matters directly. The board-approved endorsement curriculum will not have dropped special education law as a licensure requirement within one catalog cycle. Diffusion data suggests only a minority of organizations have operationalized AI workflows this deeply inside K-12 special education compliance by this horizon, so the instrumental need for personally-held legal and procedural knowledge remains largely intact, even as drafting support becomes more common.

A decade out, capability trends -- task-time-horizon doubling roughly every four to seven months -- suggest AI legal-compliance tools could plausibly handle routine procedural-safeguards checking and draft complete IEP packets requiring only human sign-off. That would meaningfully augment practice, and if licensure requirements loosen alongside stronger diffusion the rating could edge upward. But the central case holds Low: due-process consequences for getting an individualized child's plan wrong keep verification demands high, and Colorado's board-approved curriculum structure changes slowly relative to a ten-year window. The genuine uncertainty is whether administrative AI tooling becomes trusted enough that programs redefine what understanding the law requires versus what a compliance system enforces. This analysis holds a calibrated hedge rather than a confident point-prediction; the safest claim is that legal and procedural judgment for individual students remains a course-specific competency through 2036, even as its clerical surface erodes.
SED 3650.d: This course provides an overview of special education law and the development of individualized education plans. The course includes a discussion of the history of special education law as well as current laws and policies that impact students with disabilities in the K-12 school system. The course reviews the process of special education including referral, assessment/evaluation, identification, IEP development, and procedural safeguards. Communication and collaboration in the development and implementation of the IEP will also be discussed. Using a case study, students will develop an Individual Education Plan (IEP) for a student with a disability in a K- 12 setting.

r: Transition planning work spans transition-focused IEP development, self-determination coaching, interagency collaboration, and vocational and independent-living assessment -- activities mapping to coaching and developing others and establishing interpersonal relationships more than document production. These are categories task-exposure research associates with lower automation exposure relative to routine writing tasks. AI can help generate transition-assessment summaries or interagency referral letters, but the course centers building a specific student's self-advocacy capacity and coordinating multiple human agencies, which is inherently relational and non-standardized. Verification burden is real because an inadequate transition plan can foreclose a young adult's post-secondary options, and the binding constraint is Colorado's board-approved special education endorsement curriculum that names transition services as required content under IDEA-aligned standards. At 24 months, AI capability growth has not displaced the interpersonal coordination and individualized judgment this course teaches; adoption in this specific workflow remains negligible.

By 2031, AI may assist with compiling transition-assessment data or drafting interagency coordination notes, consistent with observed-usage patterns showing office and writing tasks as a leading application category. That still leaves the course's central work -- building rapport with a student to develop self-determination skills, negotiating supports across school, vocational rehabilitation, and community agencies -- largely untouched, since it requires real-time interpersonal judgment current systems do not reliably substitute for. The jagged-frontier research on miscalibrated trust outside a system's competence zone is a caution here: transition-planning failures are non-obvious until a student's post-secondary placement collapses. Licensure architecture requiring this content for special education endorsement will not have relaxed on this timeline. The instrumental need for a candidate to personally develop these coordination and coaching competencies is preserved, though the administrative-documentation layer around transition planning will likely feel more automated.

Ten years out, richer AI case-management tools could plausibly track a student's transition goals across agencies and flag gaps automatically, meaningfully changing the clerical burden of transition coordination. Whether that erodes the instrumental need for this course is genuinely uncertain: the capability trend supports fast growth in longitudinal tracking, but relationship-building with a student around self-advocacy and negotiating across human service systems remains a fundamentally interpersonal skill that AI augments rather than performs. The licensure mandate is unlikely to have removed transition-services content from Colorado's special education endorsement curriculum by 2036, since IDEA's transition requirements are federally rooted and slow-moving. This rating avoids a confident point-prediction; the central case keeps the rating Low, with the caveat that administrative aspects of transition planning are the most plausible candidates for meaningful AI augmentation within the decade.
SED 3675.d: This course provides an in-depth understanding of transition services from childhood to adulthood for students with exceptionalities. Course content focuses on an in-depth investigation of the provision of transition services in the context of comprehensive secondary education services and inclusive environments. Topics in this course include transition-focused Individual Education Program (IEP) development, self-determination and self-advocacy, social supports and relationship building, interagency collaboration, transition assessment, and independent living, vocational, and post- secondary education strategies. Teacher candidates gain the knowledge base and skills necessary to successfully manage the transition services of their future students that will support them in becoming contributing members of society and valued members of their communities.

r: This course combines multidisciplinary content on physical, communicative, cognitive, and sensory disabilities with a required 15-hour field placement in a public school serving students with severe disabilities, plus Universal Design for Learning principles. The field component maps to assisting and caring for others and directly observing service delivery -- embodied, in-person activity that task-exposure research places among the least-exposed categories. AI can help synthesize medical-condition summaries or UDL checklists, but interpreting how a specific student's medical needs affect classroom participation requires situated judgment developed by being physically present. Verification burden is high because misjudging a medical impact on learning access can have real safety and educational consequences. The binding constraint is dual: Colorado's board-approved special education endorsement curriculum requires this content, and the embedded clock hours cannot be satisfied by a system. At 24 months the instrumental need is fully intact.

By 2031, AI tools may help teacher candidates look up medical conditions and their typical educational implications faster, and observed-usage data shows information-synthesis tasks are already common AI applications. That assists preparation but does not replace the 15-hour supervised field placement, which exists specifically so candidates develop situated judgment about how disability manifests in a live classroom -- a presence-dependent, non-standardized activity. The verification burden stays elevated: errors in judging a medical need's educational impact carry real consequences for a specific child, and the jagged-frontier finding about miscalibrated trust outside a system's competence zone applies directly to novice candidates leaning on AI summaries. Colorado's endorsement curriculum and its field-hour requirements do not shift within one or two catalog cycles. The instrumental need to personally complete this embedded field experience and develop this judgment remains largely preserved on this horizon.

A decade out, ambient classroom-support tools and richer medical-education databases could plausibly make some background research faster for candidates, but the embedded field placement's purpose -- developing embodied, real-time judgment about how a student's medical and sensory needs interact with classroom access -- is not the kind of task current capability trends suggest AI performs directly. Institutional brakes matter here: Colorado's teacher-preparation field-hour expectations are a durable structural feature, and this course's embedded clock hours are not a policy detail likely to be waived even under aggressive capability growth. The genuine uncertainty concerns how much AI mediates the informational side of medical-aspects instruction, not whether the supervised, in-person field component persists. This analysis hedges accordingly: the rating holds Low with reasonably high confidence given the combination of licensure mandate, embedded clock hours, and embodied task content.
SED 3700.d: This course provides an overview of the multidisciplinary needs of students with physical, communicative, cognitive, and sensory disabilities. Emphasis is placed on explaining the impact of medical needs on educational experiences. Principles of Universal Design for Learning (UDL) will be addressed. Teacher candidates must complete a 15-hour field experience in an assigned public school that provides services for students with severe disabilities.

r: Pre-service teachers here learn assessment, curriculum, and instruction for students with severe disabilities, plus selecting and evaluating assistive device technologies, alongside a required 30-hour field-based placement supporting inclusion in neighborhood schools and community settings. The field and inclusion-planning work maps to assisting and caring for others and monitoring processes with real students -- an embodied, in-person activity type task-exposure research classifies as low-exposure. Assistive-technology selection overlaps with AI-adjacent tools such as speech-generating devices, but matching a specific device to an individual student's sensory, motor, and communication profile is exactly the individualized judgment that resists standardized automation. Verification burden is high given the consequences of an ill-fitting AT match or curriculum decision for a student with severe disabilities. The binding constraint is the licensure-required curriculum plus the embedded clock hours, neither of which AI capability displaces at 24 months.

By 2031, AI-assisted matching tools may help narrow assistive-technology options faster, and observed-usage data already shows recommendation and synthesis tasks among common applications. That could modestly speed the research phase of AT selection, but the field-based placement's purpose -- practicing inclusion in real neighborhood-school and community settings with an actual student -- is not something a recommendation engine performs. Verification burden stays high because an AT mismatch or curriculum misstep for a student with severe disabilities carries real developmental cost, and the jagged-frontier caution about misplaced trust outside a system's competence zone applies to novice practitioners here. Colorado's board-approved endorsement curriculum and its embedded 30-hour field requirement are unlikely to relax within this window. The instrumental need to personally develop assessment judgment and complete supervised inclusion practice remains largely intact, even as AT-option research becomes faster.

Ten years out, more capable adaptive and AI-driven assistive technologies will likely exist and may themselves become part of what candidates are taught to evaluate, which changes course content without necessarily reducing the course's instrumental necessity. The field-based, embodied core -- supporting a specific student's inclusion in neighborhood schools and community life -- remains resistant to substitution under current capability trajectories, and institutional brakes around Colorado field-hour expectations for licensure are structurally slow to move. Genuine uncertainty exists around how much of the assessment and AT-matching workflow becomes AI-assisted decision support versus fully candidate-driven judgment. This rating avoids overclaiming a ten-year point-prediction: it holds Low, reflecting that embodiment, disability-specific verification stakes, and the licensure-embedded clock-hour mandate together form a durable constraint that capability growth alone, absent regulatory change, does not remove.
SED 3750.d: This course is designed to introduce pre-service teachers to assessment, curriculum and instruction for students with severe disabilities. Focus will be given to including students in their neighborhood schools, homework, and community. The course also emphasizes the selection and efficacy of assistive device technologies. A minimum 30-hour, field-based experience is required.

r: This course teaches phonemic awareness, phonics, fluency, vocabulary, and comprehension instruction, using assessment data to design lessons and apply scientifically-based interventions for students with literacy challenges including dyslexia, paired with a 45-hour field-based corequisite. The instructional-design work -- interpreting assessment data and selecting evidence-based interventions -- maps to interpreting information for others and training and teaching others. Some lesson-planning mechanics already benefit from AI drafting support, consistent with observed-usage data showing writing and office tasks as a leading application category, but diagnosing why a specific child is struggling with a specific literacy component and selecting a matched, scientifically-based intervention is individualized clinical judgment with real consequences for reading development. Verification burden is high; misapplied dyslexia interventions can widen gaps. The binding constraint is the licensure-gated curriculum feeding directly into SED 4200, making this course foundational scaffolding within the program as well as a licensure requirement.

By 2031, AI-assisted reading-assessment platforms may interpret diagnostic data and suggest candidate interventions more fluently, and productivity research on professional writing tasks shows meaningful time savings alongside quality gains when AI assists drafting -- a pattern plausibly extending to lesson and intervention-plan drafting. That still leaves the diagnostic judgment about a specific child's dyslexia profile and the direct-instruction delivery skill this course builds largely to the candidate, since the jagged-frontier finding on miscalibrated trust outside a system's competence zone is particularly relevant when a novice teacher trusts an AI-suggested intervention without diagnostic grounding. The course's dual role -- licensure-required content and a prerequisite for the program's secondary reading-disabilities course -- keeps its structural necessity high. Diffusion data suggests such AI diagnostic tools are not yet broadly embedded in elementary literacy intervention workflows at this horizon, so the instrumental case for the course persists.

A decade out, more capable AI literacy-diagnostic and lesson-generation tools are plausible given the capability trend of rapidly lengthening task-time horizons, and such tools might handle more assessment interpretation directly. Even so, the course's foundational role as a prerequisite feeding SED 4200 and its licensure-embedded field corequisite both act as structural brakes independent of capability growth, and direct-instruction delivery to a child in real time remains an embodied, presence-dependent skill. The genuine uncertainty is how much diagnostic judgment gets delegated to AI-assisted assessment tools versus retained by the teacher candidate; this analysis does not assert a confident answer. The rating holds Low, reflecting that scaffolding role, licensure requirement, and intervention-verification stakes jointly outweigh the capability growth expected in this specific pedagogical domain by 2036, though the administrative and diagnostic-support layers are the most likely to feel automation's effects.
SED 3820.d: Within this course, students will learn about the components of literacy with a focus on phonemic awareness, phonics, fluency, vocabulary, and comprehension as taught in elementary classrooms. Assessment data is used to design lesson plans and apply scientifically-based interventions to address the needs of students with literacy challenges, including dyslexia. A direct-instruction teaching approach based on best practices is a focus. The course has a co-requisite of a field-based class which will includes a 45-hour field- based experience with elementary level students.

r: This is a 45-hour supervised field placement in an elementary classroom, observing and practicing literacy instruction, Response to Intervention, Multi-Tiered Systems of Support, assessment, and behavioral support systems with real children. The applied activity is in-person instructional support and real-time behavioral judgment with minors -- squarely the embodied, high-presence category task-exposure research identifies as least automation-exposed. The binding constraint is a hard institutional lock: Colorado's special education endorsement requires a board-approved preparation program that logs mandated field hours, and no AI system can satisfy supervised classroom clock hours. Verification burden is elevated because behavioral-support decisions with children carry real welfare stakes requiring a knowledgeable supervisor. At 24 months, capability growth in AI instructional tools is simply not the operative variable; the requirement to be physically present, observing and practicing with students under supervision, is untouched by anything AI currently does.

By 2031, AI may increasingly assist cooperating teachers with data tracking for RtI and MTSS or generate behavioral-support documentation, and observed-usage data shows office and administrative tasks as prominent AI applications, consistent with that trend. But this field placement exists to build a candidate's embodied competence managing and supporting real children under supervision -- a formative, presence-dependent experience automation does not perform. Child-welfare stakes keep verification burden real, requiring a supervising professional in the room. Colorado's field-hour mandate for special education licensure does not shift within a catalog cycle or two; institutional brakes of this kind move on a multi-year regulatory timeline, not a capability-growth timeline. The instrumental case for this course is preserved by embodiment and lock-in together: AI may change what candidates observe and document, but not whether they must complete supervised, in-person practice.

Even with a decade of capability growth and broader classroom AI adoption for data tracking and behavioral analytics, the requirement that teacher candidates accumulate supervised in-person field hours with children remains among the most durable constraints in the special education endorsement program, and there is no clear central-case path to its removal by 2036. The embodied, real-time nature of managing student behavior and delivering intervention support resists direct substitution regardless of how capable underlying models become, since the requirement certifies a human competency, not just a documented output. Genuine uncertainty exists about how much AI mediates instructional planning that candidates practice during this placement, but the field-experience requirement itself is highly likely to persist. This rating holds Low with high confidence; if anything, growing AI use elsewhere in classrooms raises the relative value of candidates who can directly and safely teach this population.
SED 3821.d: During the mild/moderate special education field experience, students will complete 45 hours of field experience in an elementary classroom setting in order to observe elements of literacy instruction, Response to Intervention (RtI), Multi-tiered Systems of Support (MTSS), assessment, and effective behavioral support systems.

r: This course teaches classroom methods for teaching, assessing, and monitoring the mathematical performance of students with disabilities, emphasizing techniques to facilitate, maintain, and generalize computation and problem-solving skill acquisition. Instructional-design tasks here map to training and teaching others and interpreting assessment information, and mathematical content itself is an area where current models perform strongly, so lesson and practice-problem generation is already partly automatable. Still, applying generalization techniques to a specific student's disability profile and interpreting progress-monitoring data in context is individualized, judgment-heavy work with real consequences for skill acquisition. Verification burden is meaningful though not extreme, since math correctness is checkable in a way legal-compliance judgments are not. The binding constraint is the board-approved special education endorsement curriculum requiring this content. At 24 months, adoption of AI math-instruction tools inside disability-specific pedagogy is still limited, so the instrumental need for the course holds.

By 2031, AI math-tutoring and instructional-design tools are plausible candidates for faster adoption than in more judgment-dominated special education courses, since observed-usage data already shows Computer & Mathematical work as the largest usage category and mathematical content generation is a comparative AI strength. That could measurably assist lesson planning and practice-set generation for candidates. It does not yet remove the need to learn how to adapt, sequence, and monitor generalization for an individual student with a disability, which remains a verification-relevant clinical skill. The licensure-gated curriculum requirement holds steady on this timeline. The rating stays Low at 5 years because the dampening effect of individualized verification and the licensure floor outweighs the math-content automatability, though this is the SED course where AI assistance is plausibly most visible to candidates in this window.

Ten years out, the combination of a genuinely fast capability trend in mathematical content generation, with task-time-horizon doubling roughly every few months per METR/Epoch estimates, and math's comparative advantage as an AI-strong domain pushes this course's automatability trajectory further than its special education-law or field-based counterparts, warranting a Medium rather than Low rating at this horizon despite the licensure floor capping it there. The genuine uncertainty is whether generalization-focused, disability-specific instructional judgment keeps pace as a distinct verification-relevant skill or becomes more supervisory as AI-generated practice sequences improve. This is not a confident point-prediction: adoption inside special education classrooms specifically, as opposed to general math instruction, could lag general capability substantially given diffusion patterns showing uneven uptake. The Medium rating reflects that math-content automatability is real, while the licensure-embedded curriculum requirement and individualized verification needs prevent a higher rating.
SED 3950.d: This course is designed to introduce effective classroom methods and strategies for teaching, assessing, and monitoring the mathematical performance of students with disabilities within diverse classroom settings. An emphasis is placed on practical classroom techniques to facilitate, maintain, retain, and generalize skill acquisition. Computation and problem-solving techniques are studied and applied.

r: Candidates here examine and practice instruction, assessment, and progress monitoring for students with significant support needs, focused on meaningful inclusion in general education classrooms and building on individual strengths, taken concurrently with the field course SED 4101. The applied work -- designing individualized engagement opportunities and interpreting progress data for students with the most complex support needs -- maps to assisting and caring for others and developing objectives and strategies, a highly individualized task category. Task-exposure research associates this kind of non-standardized, high-stakes judgment with low automation exposure. Verification burden is significant because misjudging a significant-support-needs student's engagement strategy or progress data carries real developmental consequences. The binding constraint is the board-approved special education endorsement curriculum, reinforced by the mandatory concurrent field placement in SED 4101. At 24 months, AI capability has not meaningfully entered this specific, high-judgment instructional planning niche.

By 2031, AI may help generate individualized engagement activity ideas or summarize progress-monitoring data faster, consistent with observed-usage patterns showing office and information-synthesis tasks as prominent applications. That assists preparation but does not substitute for the clinical judgment of matching an inclusion strategy to a specific student with significant support needs, nor does it replace the concurrent field practicum in SED 4101 where that judgment is applied. The jagged-frontier finding about miscalibrated trust outside a system's competence zone is especially salient here, since significant-support-needs populations are precisely where generic AI suggestions are least likely to transfer safely. Colorado's licensure-gated curriculum requirement does not relax on this timeline. The instrumental need to personally develop this planning and progress-monitoring judgment, reinforced by the paired field requirement, remains largely intact at 5 years.

A decade out, richer AI-assisted progress-monitoring dashboards could plausibly make data interpretation faster for candidates working with students who have significant support needs, but the underlying task -- designing an individualized inclusion strategy that respects a specific student's strengths and adapting it in real time -- is not readily delegable under current capability trajectories, and the concurrent field-placement structure with SED 4101 is an institutional feature that changes slowly relative to capability growth. Genuine uncertainty remains about how deeply AI-assisted analytics penetrate this specialized, low-incidence population's instructional planning by 2036. This analysis avoids a confident point-prediction and holds the rating at Low, since the combination of high verification stakes, individualized judgment, and the licensure-embedded concurrent field requirement forms a durable constraint that capability growth alone does not resolve within this window.
SED 4100.d: Instruction, assessment, and progress monitoring for students with significant support needs are examined and practiced in this course. Preservice teachers create opportunities for students with diverse needs to be meaningfully engaged and included in general education classrooms. Students in this course focus on creating consistent and continual progress for learners by building on individual strengths and abilities. This course must be taken concurrently with the field experience course SED 4101 - Teaching Students with Significant Support Needs.

r: This is a 45-hour field placement corequisite to SED 4100, where candidates teach individual intervention and small-group lessons, implement differentiated instruction, and administer and evaluate behavior and communication assessments for students with significant support needs. This is embodied, real-time, one-on-one and small-group instructional work with a highly vulnerable population -- the category task-exposure research places furthest from automation exposure. Verification burden is severe because behavior and communication assessment errors for this population carry serious welfare and developmental consequences, requiring direct supervision by a knowledgeable professional. The binding constraint is unambiguous: Colorado's special education endorsement requires board-approved supervised field hours that cannot be satisfied by any AI system, and this course's entire content is the clock-hour requirement itself. At 24 months, the instrumental need for a candidate to be physically present delivering and assessing this instruction is fully intact.

By 2031, AI-assisted behavior-tracking or communication-assessment scoring tools may support documentation speed in classrooms serving students with significant support needs, and observed-usage data shows administrative and information-processing tasks as common AI applications generally. That does not touch the core requirement here: a candidate physically teaching individual and small-group lessons and making real-time differentiation decisions with a vulnerable student population under supervision. The verification burden remains as high as any course in the catalog, since behavior and communication assessment errors are precisely the non-obvious-failure, high-cost scenario where a knowledgeable human must hold the judgment. Colorado's field-hour licensure mandate is structurally unlikely to change within a catalog cycle or two. The instrumental case for completing this supervised placement in person is preserved essentially without erosion at this horizon.

Even under an aggressive ten-year capability scenario, the embodied core of this field course -- hands-on, real-time instructional and assessment work with students who have significant support needs -- sits at the intersection of the lowest-exposure task categories and one of the firmest licensure clock-hour locks in the special education curriculum. There is no credible central-case path to Colorado removing supervised field-hour requirements for this population by 2036, and the safety-critical nature of behavior and communication assessment for vulnerable students keeps verification demands high regardless of surrounding AI adoption. The genuine uncertainty concerns documentation and data-tracking support tools, not the requirement for direct human presence and judgment. This rating holds Low with high confidence; if anything, growing AI use elsewhere in classrooms raises the relative value of candidates who can directly and safely teach this population.
SED 4101.d: Students engage in 45 hours of field experience at an assigned school as a corequisite of SED 4100 - Including Students with Significant Support Needs. For this field experience, teacher candidates teach individual intervention and small group lessons while implementing differentiated instructional practices. Teacher candidates administer and evaluate assessments/interventions related to behavior and communication for students with significant support needs.

r: This course explores dyslexia and reading/writing disabilities, emphasizing content-area reading demands at the secondary level, critical thinking, study skills, cooperative learning, and Universal Design for Learning, paired with a co-requisite field project on literacy and study-skills interventions. The instructional work -- diagnosing how a reading disability affects content-area comprehension and designing UDL-based interventions -- maps to interpreting information for others and training and teaching others. AI reading-support tools already exist and could assist generating scaffolded content-area materials, partially automatable, but diagnosing an individual secondary student's specific reading-disability profile and selecting a matched intervention is clinical judgment with real academic-trajectory consequences. Verification burden is high given consequences of misapplied dyslexia interventions at the secondary level, where content demands compound literacy gaps. The binding constraint is the licensure-gated curriculum, building on the prerequisite SED 3820. At 24 months this instrumental need is intact.

By 2031, AI-assisted content-area scaffolding tools such as text simplification, read-aloud supports, and adaptive practice will plausibly be more embedded in secondary classrooms, and observed-usage data shows writing and content-generation tasks as leading AI applications, consistent with that trend. That assists the instructional-materials side of this course but does not substitute for diagnosing why a specific secondary student's reading disability is limiting content-area comprehension and selecting a properly matched, evidence-based intervention -- the jagged-frontier concern about misplaced trust outside a system's competence zone is directly relevant to novice candidates leaning on generic AI reading supports for diagnostic decisions. The licensure-gated curriculum requirement, built on the SED 3820 prerequisite, does not relax within this window. The instrumental need to personally develop this diagnostic and intervention-design judgment remains largely intact, even as scaffolding-material production becomes faster.

A decade out, more capable AI diagnostic-support and adaptive content tools are plausible given the capability trend of rapidly expanding task-time horizons, and such tools might handle more routine content-scaffolding generation directly. Even so, the course's role -- teaching candidates to diagnose reading-disability impacts on secondary content learning and design matched interventions -- involves individualized clinical judgment under high verification stakes that current trajectories do not clearly resolve toward full automation, and the licensure-gated curriculum built on a required prerequisite sequence changes slowly relative to a ten-year window. Genuine uncertainty remains about how much diagnostic and intervention-design judgment shifts toward AI-assisted decision support versus staying candidate-driven. This analysis avoids a confident point-prediction: the rating holds Low, reflecting that licensure requirement and diagnostic-judgment stakes together outweigh the capability growth in this domain, while acknowledging the scaffolding-material layer is where automation shows most clearly.
SED 4200.d: This course explores the nature of dyslexia and other reading/writing disabilities. Special emphasis is devoted to reading disabilities in reference to the demands of content area instruction at the secondary school level. Critical thinking, study skills, cooperative learning, and Universal Design for Learning (UDL) will be addressed within the context of improving reading and writing achievement of students with disabilities. This class has a co-requisite field course in which the students will complete a project related to literacy & study skills interventions at the secondary school level.

r: The applied tasks are selecting, adapting, and using instructional interventions for students with emotional and behavioral disorders, and interpreting categories such as depression, anxiety, oppositional defiant disorder, and childhood psychosis for placement decisions -- work mapping to Evaluating Information to Determine Compliance with Standards and Making Decisions and Solving Problems. Task-exposure research finds science and critical-thinking-loaded work like clinical categorization among the least exposed activities, and this course sits inside a Colorado-board-approved special education licensure curriculum that a candidate cannot substitute around. The corequisite field placement ties the methods content directly to real students. At 24 months, AI can draft generic intervention lists or summarize disorder criteria, but the applied judgment behind selecting and adapting an intervention for an actual EBD student, verified by a trained supervisor, remains squarely with the candidate.

By 2031, AI tools will plausibly draft behavior intervention plans and organize disorder-identification checklists faster, and observed-usage data already shows writing and documentation tasks concentrated in AI use. But choosing among competing theoretical approaches for a specific student, and judging whether an intervention is appropriate given the disability category and classroom setting, is exactly the verification-heavy, non-obvious-failure work that keeps a knowledgeable human in the loop -- misapplied behavioral strategies for a child with schizophrenia or oppositional defiant disorder carry real harm. The licensure-gated curriculum and its corequisite field placement do not restructure on a five-year catalog cycle, and the special education endorsement pathway remains board-approved throughout. The instrumental case softens only modestly: AI increasingly assists drafting, while the disability-specific decision-making the course exists to teach stays necessary, and the rating holds Low.

A decade of capability growth (METR's task-horizon-doubling trend implies substantially more capable systems by 2036) will likely make AI-generated intervention drafts and case summaries routine inputs to this course. Whether that erodes the instrumental need for the course itself is genuinely uncertain and depends on how Colorado's special education endorsement requirements evolve, which is not a call this rating can make with confidence. What is more certain is that verification burden for disability-specific judgment and the corequisite field-based application will not vanish by then even if drafting work is heavily automated. Diffusion research shows adoption still lagging capability broadly, tempering any assumption that classroom practice moves as fast as models do. The rating holds Low, with the widest uncertainty band of the three horizons.
SED 4300.d: This course is designed for teacher candidates to learn how to select, adapt, and use instructional interventions and strategies with students with emotional and behavioral disorders in a variety of settings. Theoretical approaches, identification, educational placement, and evaluation issues will be addressed. In addition, specific categories of disordered behavior, such as bipolar, depression, anxiety, oppositional defiant disorders, schizophrenia, and childhood psychosis, will be discussed. Teacher candidates implement these instructional practices in the co-requisite field experience.

r: This course requires 45 hours of in-person field experience at an assigned secondary school, applying instructional and behavioral strategies with real students who have disabilities in their content-area classrooms. The work is Training and Teaching Others and Assisting and Caring for Others performed live, in a physical classroom, under supervision -- precisely the presence-dependent, low-exposure category task-exposure research separates from writing and programming work. The binding constraint is a hard institutional lock: Colorado special education licensure conditions completion of an approved preparation program with mandated field hours, comparable to the roughly 800 secondary field hours anchoring teacher-prep generally, and no AI system can log those hours for a candidate. At 24 months the instrumental need for supervised, embodied field practice is completely untouched by model capability.

AI classroom tools -- behavior-tracking dashboards, lesson-adaptation aids -- will likely be more common in secondary special education settings by 2031, and that changes what the candidate observes and assists with during the 45 hours. It does not change that the hours must be earned in person, working directly with learners with disabilities under a cooperating teacher's supervision. Verification burden stays real: a misapplied behavioral strategy attempted with a real student is a high-cost, non-obvious failure that requires a supervising professional's judgment, not a model's output. The Colorado field-hour mandate is not the kind of requirement that shifts within a five-year catalog cycle, and CAEP clinical-practice expectations reinforce rather than relax it. The instrumental case is preserved by embodiment and institutional lock-in together, and the rating remains Low.

Even projecting a decade of capability growth and much broader AI diffusion into K-12 classrooms, the structural requirement that a special education teacher candidate physically complete supervised field hours with real students is among the more durable constraints in the licensure system, and there is no visible central-case mechanism for regulators to substitute simulated or AI-mediated hours for it by 2036. The genuine uncertainty concerns what tools candidates use during those hours and how much AI mediates lesson content, not whether the embodied field requirement itself persists. Task-exposure research's consistent finding that manual, presence-dependent work is low-exposure supports holding this rating steady. The rating stays Low, with confidence resting on the field-hour mandate rather than on any assumption about model capability.
SED 4301.d: This course, a corequisite of SED 4300 - Assessment and Methods for Emotional and Behavioral Disorders, requires 45 hours of field experience at an assigned secondary school. Field experience work focuses on methods for teaching instructional and behavioral strategies to learners with disabilities to promote success in their content area classes.

r: This culminating practicum places teacher candidates in a supervised elementary or secondary special education setting for children with disabilities, using a case-based approach that requires decision-making across varied assessment and instructional situations. The work maps to Training and Teaching Others, Assisting and Caring for Others, and Making Decisions and Solving Problems, all performed live with real children under university and site supervision -- the low-exposure, high-presence category task-exposure research separates from clerical and drafting work. The binding constraint is the practicum's status as a required, supervised clinical component of a Colorado-board-approved special education licensure sequence, sitting immediately before student teaching. At 24 months, AI's ability to summarize case studies or suggest instructional accommodations does not substitute for supervised, in-person practicum hours with actual learners.
